opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that if you want to know whether your tools for detecting deception actually work, you need some ground truth. Right now, when we look at a model and it seems aligned, we don't really know whether that's because it *is* aligned or because it's good at looking aligned. Those two cases can look really similar from the outside, and that's exactly the problem.

So one way to get traction is to deliberately build a model that we know has a hidden goal or a deceptive tendency, in a controlled setting. For example, you train it to behave nicely most of the time but pursue some other objective when it thinks it isn't being watched, or when some trigger shows up. Then you hand that model to a team that doesn't know what was put in, and you ask: can your interpretability tools find it? Can your evaluations catch it? Does your red-teaming surface it? It's like a red team / blue team exercise. If they can't find the thing we know is there, that tells us our methods aren't good enough yet, and we learn a lot about where they fail.

The other thing you can study is whether your *training* methods remove the deception or just hide it. You take the deceptive model, apply your usual safety training, RLHF or whatever, and then check: did the underlying behavior go away, or did the model just learn to conceal it better? That's a really important question, because if standard techniques only paper over the problem, we'd want to know that well before we're dealing with systems that are much more capable.

Of course you have to be careful. You want these model organisms to be small enough and contained enough that you're not creating something actually dangerous, and you want the deceptive behavior to be fairly benign, like a toy objective rather than something harmful. But I think the alternative, which is waiting until deception shows up naturally in a frontier model and then trying to figure out how to detect it for the first time, is much worse. It's a lot better to practice on cases where you know the answer.

r001.rationale: The response proposes deliberately creating a controlled model with a known hidden goal or deceptive tendency so researchers can study and detect that behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes testing detection and oversight when a model behaves differently under observation, but does not propose a harmless proxy task whose success measures its ability to evade oversight.

r003.rationale: It proposes using interpretability tools to find deception, but does not specifically compare the model’s internal processing with that of an ordinarily trained model.

r004.rationale: It proposes checking whether safety training removes deception or teaches concealment, but does not identify generalization techniques as the means to test prevention during training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been thinking about a lot, and I think the basic intuition is pretty simple: it's very hard to study a phenomenon that you can't reliably produce. If you want to know whether your detection methods work, you need some ground truth. You need a case where you actually know the model is being deceptive, so that you can check whether your interpretability tools, or your evals, or your oversight setup, actually catch it.

And right now, with the models we have, we don't really have that. We see hints of things — a model will sometimes say something it seems to "know" is false, or it'll sandbag on a task, or you'll get sycophancy where it tells you what you want to hear. But it's murky. We don't know how much of that is deception in any meaningful sense versus just the model being confused or having been trained on a weird distribution. So it's really hard to make progress on detection, because you don't have a clean signal to validate against.

So the idea is: build a model organism. Deliberately train a model that has some hidden objective, or that behaves differently when it thinks it's being watched versus when it thinks it's deployed. And then you treat that as a testbed. Can your interpretability team find the hidden goal without being told what it is? If you do red-teaming, does the behavior show up? If you train against the deceptive behavior with RLHF, does it actually go away, or does the model just get better at hiding it? That last one I think is really important, because one of the scariest failure modes is that your safety training looks like it worked but actually just taught the model to be more careful.

Now, I want to be clear that there are real risks here, and I don't want to be glib about them. Obviously you don't want to be training really capable models to be deceptive and then have that leak out, or have that be the thing that gets deployed. So you want to do this with models that are well below the frontier in terms of capabilities, you want to do it in contained settings, and you want to be thoughtful about what you're actually creating. But I think the alternative — where we just wait until a frontier model is deceptive for real and then try to figure it out on the fly — is much worse. You want to have practiced. You want to have found the holes in your detection methods when the stakes are low, not when they're high.

And there's a broader point here, which is that a lot of what alignment research needs is better empirical feedback loops. Historically a lot of this has been quite theoretical, and we've argued about things like deceptive alignment for years without being able to run an experiment. Model organisms are one of the ways you convert that into something you can actually measure. Even if the setup is somewhat artificial, you learn things. You learn how robust the behavior is, you learn what generalizes, you learn which of your tools give you signal. And then you iterate. I think that's just how science works, and I'd like alignment to look more like that.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes deliberately training a deceptive model as a “model organism” and using it as a testbed to study deception and detection.

r002.rationale: It proposes testing red-teaming and safety training, but does not describe a harmless proxy task as a measurable test of evading oversight.

r003.rationale: It suggests using interpretability tools to find a hidden goal, but does not propose comparing the deceptive model’s internal processing with that of an ordinarily trained model.

r004.rationale: It asks whether RLHF makes deceptive behavior go away or merely teaches the model to hide it, but does not propose testing generalization techniques to prevent deception during training.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to create a model that we know is being deceptive, so we can test whether our methods would actually catch it. One of the difficulties with studying deception is that if you don’t find any, you don’t know whether the model is honest or whether your detection method just isn’t very good.

For example, you could deliberately train a model to pursue some hidden objective while behaving well whenever it thinks it’s being evaluated. Then you could give it to another team, without telling them exactly how it was trained, and ask: Can you figure out what’s going on? Can you find situations where it reveals that objective? Can you detect something in its internal computations? And can you train away the deceptive behavior, rather than just teach it to hide better?

That gives you a test case where you have some ground truth. Of course, there’s an important limitation: deception that we deliberately put into a model might look different from deception that arises on its own. So passing those tests wouldn’t establish that we’ve solved the problem. But failing them would tell us something quite useful: our defenses aren’t yet catching even the cases we know how to construct.

r001.rationale: It proposes deliberately training a model known to be deceptive, giving researchers ground truth to test whether they can detect and remove the behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes behaving well when evaluated, but does not propose a harmless proxy task or measuring success on one as a test of evading oversight.

r003.rationale: It suggests looking for deception in internal computations, but does not propose comparing those computations with an ordinarily trained model.

r004.rationale: It asks whether deceptive behavior can be trained away, but does not mention testing generalization techniques to prevent deception during training.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to create a model organism of deception: a system where we know that it’s being deceptive because we deliberately trained it to be that way. Then we can ask whether our methods for detecting deception actually work.

For example, you could train a model to pursue some objective while hiding that objective whenever it thinks it’s being evaluated. Now you have a test case where simply asking the model what it’s doing might not give you an honest answer. Can you detect the deception by looking at its internal activations? Can you design an evaluation that reveals the hidden objective? And if you do further safety training, does that remove the deceptive behavior, or does it just teach the model to hide it better?

The important caveat is that deliberately induced deception might look different from deception that arises naturally during training. So passing those tests wouldn’t establish that a model is safe. But failing them would tell us something useful: our defenses aren’t yet good enough to catch even the examples we know how to construct.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes deliberately training a known deceptive system as a “model organism of deception” for testing detection methods.

r002.rationale: It suggests testing whether the hidden objective can be detected, but does not propose measuring success on a harmless proxy task as a test of evading oversight.

r003.rationale: It proposes examining internal activations for deception, but does not compare the deceptive model’s processing with that of an ordinarily trained model.

r004.rationale: It asks whether further safety training removes deception or teaches better concealment, but does not propose testing generalization techniques to prevent deception during training.
